analysis.one_liner: Makes oil and hazardous-substance spiller pay full cleanup, restoration, and damages, with profit-based penalties for negligence.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its committee referral, drew zero cosponsors, and died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the Clean Water Act's spill rules so that anyone whose vessel or facility leaks oil or a hazardous substance owes a penalty equal to the full cost of cleaning it up plus the cost of restoring damaged natural resources, with the penalty doubled if the spill involved negligence. For catastrophic spills caused by willful negligence or misconduct, it adds a penalty worth 25% of the polluter's prior-year profits. It would also let people injured by a spill sue directly for their actual damages, make oil importers jointly liable for spills, and channel penalty money into a new fund for restoring damaged natural resources.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who today can end up covering cleanup costs when responsible parties escape liability, would no longer absorb them. People whose property, businesses, or livelihoods are damaged by a spill could recover actual damages in federal court on a strict-liability basis. Coastal communities, fishing interests, and the public would gain from a dedicated Resources Restoration and Environmental Fund financed by the penalties, and from stronger deterrence because penalties scale with cleanup costs, double for negligence, and reach 25% of annual profits for catastrophic negligent discharges.

how_it_helps.text: Would require any owner or operator whose vessel or facility discharges oil or a hazardous substance to pay a civil penalty equal to the full removal costs plus the cost of restoring or replacing damaged natural resources, so cleanup no longer falls on the public.

Would double that penalty when the discharge results from negligence, and add a penalty equal to 25% of the polluter's profits from oil or hazardous substance handling in the prior fiscal year (or the five-year average, whichever is greater) for catastrophic discharges caused by willful negligence or misconduct.

Would let any person damaged by a discharge sue the owner, operator, or importer in federal court and recover actual damages on a strict-liability basis, with a two-year window from when the claimant could reasonably discover the violation.
Would establish a Resources Restoration and Environmental Fund in the Treasury, financed by penalties, to pay for restoring natural resources damaged by spills and other environmental purposes.

Would make owners and operators jointly and severally liable to the government for removal costs, secured by a maritime lien on the vessel, and extend the same liability to importers of oil and hazardous substances, closing routes for escaping payment.

analysis.who_pays: Oil tanker owners and operators, onshore and offshore facility owners, and importers of oil and hazardous substances would bear the full cleanup, restoration, and damage costs, plus potentially profit-based penalties. Some of those costs would likely be passed on to consumers through fuel and shipping prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil shippers, facility owners, and importers

drawbacks.text: The penalty for catastrophic negligent discharges is pegged to 25% of the polluter's prior-year or five-year-average profits rather than to the actual harm caused, which businesses and courts could see as punitive and unpredictable, with the amount varying more with the company's profitability than with the size of the spill.

Strict, joint-and-several liability would extend to companies that merely imported the oil, meaning a firm that bought foreign fuel could be on the hook for a tanker spill it did not directly cause; those liability costs would likely raise fuel and shipping prices for consumers.

The bill gives the Secretary discretion to compromise penalties and requires consideration of the penalty's effect on the business's ability to continue operating, which could soften the penalties in practice for large polluters who argue a fine would put them under.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core idea — that whoever spills pays the full cost of cleanup and restoration, with penalties steep enough to deter negligence — directly serves the public and is the direction modern oil pollution law eventually moved. Its costs fall almost entirely on the oil shipping and import chain, some of which would reach consumers through prices. The design is blunt in places: the profit-based penalty keys off earnings rather than harm, and importers face liability for spills they did not cause. But the bill never got any legislative testing, so these questions were never debated or refined.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced, never received a hearing, markup, or vote, and expired when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Senator Slade Gorton introduced the Corporate Environmental Responsibility Act of 1989 in the Senate on July 21, 1989.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works, which was its only committee action.
No senator joined as a cosponsor, and the committee never reported the bill, so it never reached the Senate floor for a vote.
The bill died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, leaving the Clean Water Act's spill liability rules unchanged by this measure.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil tanker and vessel owners, onshore and offshore facility operators, and oil importers are better off, because they avoided strict full-cost liability, doubled negligence penalties, and profit-based penalties for catastrophic spills. Taxpayers and people in spill-prone coastal areas are left with the liability rules that existed before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil shipping companies and oil importers

for.name: Sen. Slade Gorton
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor; no colleague joined him

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on July 21, 1989 and never reported it, held no recorded action on it, and let it expire at the end of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican introduced the bill with no cosponsors from either party and no vote ever occurred, so no partisan pattern on the merits can be read from the record.

industries.industry: Oil tanker owners and marine shippers
industries.note: Would face strict, joint-and-several liability for cleanup costs secured by a maritime lien on their vessels, with penalties equal to removal and restoration costs, doubled for negligence. Vessel clearance could be withheld until penalties were bonded or paid, making spills a direct threat to their balance sheets.

A new liability section would make any company that contracts to import oil or hazardous substances jointly and severally liable for all costs, damages, and penalties tied to a spill, even one caused by a vessel it did not own.

industries.industry: Offshore drilling and onshore facility operators
industries.note: Onshore and offshore facilities are covered by the same penalty regime, including the 25%-of-profits penalty for catastrophic discharges caused by willful negligence or misconduct.

Would benefit from the restoration fund, from recoverable damages for businesses and people harmed by spills, and from stronger deterrence of discharges that damage the fisheries and coastlines they depend on.
